I am a political scientist currently on the job market. I received my PhD in Political Science from UC Riverside in 2024, where my dissertation examined the politics of student loan debt. Most recently, I was a postdoctoral researcher at Université Laval, where I worked on the PASI immigrant integration panel study. I also have a Master’s in Public Policy from the UC Riverside School of Public Policy, where my master’s project dealt with eviction rates and public transit access in low-income areas of Riverside County.
My research explores how personal debt impacts political attitudes in the American context, as well as immigration and immigrant political attitudes both in the American context and comparatively. I also use naturalistic data from online platforms like Yelp and Google Reviews to study how political events shape everyday behavior. Methodologically, my interests include text as data, social media data, and survey design.
Before grad school, I served with AmeriCorps in South-Central Los Angeles and briefly taught English in Beijing. In my spare time, I read widely, write fiction, and run more slowly than I’d like.

title: Research
text:
Current Projects

Naturalistic Data and Political Attitudes
I am currently working on a series of projects that use naturalistic data from online platforms, particularly Yelp and Google Reviews, to capture political attitudes and behaviors as they occur organically, outside of traditional survey settings.
Group Threat and Solidarity: Evidence from Yelp Reviews of Mexican Restaurants (with Adam Hobbs and Loren Collingwood) examines how partisan and racial attitudes manifest in online reviews of Mexican restaurants, using Yelp data to capture affective polarization in everyday consumer behavior. Under review.
BLM Protests and Online Reviews of Black-Owned Businesses (with Adam Hobbs, Deren Onursal, and Tre Garnett) investigates whether Black Lives Matter protests generate solidarity or backlash toward Black-owned businesses, using Yelp and Google Reviews data matched with protest event data from ACLED. We find that Black-owned businesses receive significantly higher ratings following nearby BLM protests, with effects that are temporally proximate and geographically local. In progress.
In the Line of Fire: Evidence of Political Shocks in Gun Retailer Online Consumer Behavior (with Stan Oklobdzija) examines how mass shootings shape consumer evaluations of gun retailers, matching geocoded mass shooting data to Yelp and Google Reviews of gun shops. Gun shops receive significantly lower ratings following nearby shootings; effects are geographically concentrated, build over the first two months before fading, and reflect changed sentiment rather than changed review volume. In progress.
Rating the Reckoning: Gender-Salience Shocks and Online Reviews of Women-Led Businesses (with Adam Hobbs) uses Google Reviews of women-led businesses to study how national gender-salience shocks shape consumer behavior. The #MeToo movement produced a slow-building increase in ratings of women-led businesses, while the polarized fight over the Kavanaugh confirmation produced a penalty, suggesting that diffuse sympathetic mobilization generates consumer solidarity while two-sided partisan conflict generates net backlash. In progress.


Housing, Race, and Voting
Home is Where the… Immigration Attitudes Are? (with Adam Hobbs) asks whether housing affordability shapes immigration attitudes, a connection Republican elites have increasingly drawn in public debate. Combining 2024 Cooperative Election Study data with ZIP-code-level affordability measures from Zillow and the Census, we find no evidence that local housing conditions directly predict immigration attitudes. A pre-registered survey experiment (n = 1,421) shows that information explicitly linking housing costs to immigration, including an elite cue from J.D. Vance, increases anti-immigration attitudes, with policy preferences shifting most among non-partisans. In progress.
Race, Party, or Both? Racially Polarized Voting After Callais (with Loren Collingwood) responds to the Supreme Court’s 2026 decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which requires Section 2 Voting Rights Act plaintiffs to show that racially polarized voting cannot be explained by partisanship. Because standard ecological inference methods cannot accommodate partisan covariates, we propose OLS ecological regression with precinct-level party registration controls and first differences, applied across 35 statewide contests in California, Florida, and North Carolina (2014-2024). Hispanic and Black voter concentration continue to predict support for minority-preferred candidates after controlling for party registration, including in same-party (Democrat-vs-Democrat) general elections where partisanship cannot explain vote choice. In progress.


PASI (Programme d’accompagnement et de soutien à l’intégration)
I am also working with a novel panel dataset on recent immigrants to Quebec, collected during my postdoctoral appointment at Université Laval. This project, funded by MIFI (Quebec’s immigration government agency), surveys participants recruited through administrative data to study the impact of initial experiences on later political and social integration and political attitudes.
This is the first panel dataset on political attitudes composed exclusively of recently arrived immigrants in Canada or the US.
Buying Love? How Government Benefits Shape Immigrant Political Attachment examines how government-provided benefits shape the political attachment of recent immigrants. Under review.
